**Matthew 1** 

*The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham.*

*2 Abraham begat Isaac; and Isaac begat Jacob; and Jacob begat Judas and his brethren;*

*3 And Judas begat Phares and Zara of Thamar; and Phares begat Esrom; and Esrom begat Aram;*

*4 And Aram begat Aminadab; and Aminadab begat Naasson; and Naasson begat Salmon;*

*5 And Salmon begat Booz of Rachab; and Booz begat Obed of Ruth; and Obed begat Jesse;*

*6 And Jesse begat David the king; and David the king begat Solomon of her that had been the wife of Urias;*

*7 And Solomon begat Roboam; and Roboam begat Abia; and Abia begat Asa;*

*8 And Asa begat Josaphat; and Josaphat begat Joram; and Joram begat Ozias;*

*9 And Ozias begat Joatham; and Joatham begat Achaz; and Achaz begat Ezekias;*

*10 And Ezekias begat Manasses; and Manasses begat Amon; and Amon begat Josias;*

*11 And Josias begat Jechonias and his brethren, about the time they were carried away to Babylon:*

*12 And after they were brought to Babylon, Jechonias begat Salathiel; and Salathiel begat Zorobabel;*

*13 And Zorobabel begat Abiud; and Abiud begat Eliakim; and Eliakim begat Azor;*

*14 And Azor begat Sadoc; and Sadoc begat Achim; and Achim begat Eliud;*

*15 And Eliud begat Eleazar; and Eleazar begat Matthan; and Matthan begat Jacob;*

*16 And Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ.*

*17 So all the generations from Abraham to David are fourteen generations; and from David until the carrying away into Babylon are fourteen generations; and from the carrying away into Babylon unto Christ are fourteen generations.*

*18 Now the birth of Jesus Christ was on this wise: When as his mother Mary was espoused to Joseph, before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost.*

*19 Then Joseph her husband, being a just man, and not willing to make her a public example, was minded to put her away privily.*

*20 But while he thought on these things, behold, the angel of the Lord appeared unto him in a dream, saying, Joseph, thou son of David, fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife: for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost.*

*21 And she shall bring forth a son, and thou shalt call his name Jesus: for he shall save his people from their sins.*

*22 Now all this was done, that it might be fulfilled which was spoken of the Lord by the prophet, saying,*

*23 Behold, a virgin shall be with child, and shall bring forth a son, and they shall call his name Emmanuel, which being interpreted is, God with us.*

*24 Then Joseph being raised from sleep did as the angel of the Lord had bidden him, and took unto him his wife:*

*25 And knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son: and he called his name Jesus.*

The Gospel of Matthew begins with the lineage of the man, Christ Jesus, the promised seed of Abraham, through the root of Jesse, the son of David, heir by right to the throne of the earthly kingdom of Judah, yet not just a man, not of this world, born of the Holy Spirit, the Son of God. Heir to all things, through whom all things were created.

Joseph, Jesus' stepfather, engaged to Mary, with thoughts of putting the pregnant fiancee away, privately, given her condition. But the angel of the Lord visits him to say that she bears God's word, the promise of a redeemer, to take away the sins of His people. Fulfilling the prophecy, preached by Isaiah:

*Behold, a virgin shall be with child, and shall bring forth a son, and they shall call his name Emmanuel, which being interpreted is, God with us.*

And Joseph took Mary for his wife, and did not lay with her until after Jesus was born, so that He may be born of a virgin.  (Note it doesn't say "never" but "till.")

**Matthew 2** 

*Now when Jesus was born in Bethlehem of Judaea in the days of Herod the king, behold, there came wise men from the east to Jerusalem,*
*2 Saying, Where is he that is born King of the Jews? for we have seen his star in the east, and are come to worship him.*
*3 When Herod the king had heard these things, he was troubled, and all Jerusalem with him.*
*4 And when he had gathered all the chief priests and scribes of the people together, he demanded of them where Christ should be born.*
*5 And they said unto him, In Bethlehem of Judaea: for thus it is written by the prophet,*
*6 And thou Bethlehem, in the land of Juda, art not the least among the princes of Juda: for out of thee shall come a Governor, that shall rule my people Israel.*
*7 Then Herod, when he had privily called the wise men, enquired of them diligently what time the star appeared.*
*8 And he sent them to Bethlehem, and said, Go and search diligently for the young child; and when ye have found him, bring me word again, that I may come and worship him also.*
*9 When they had heard the king, they departed; and, lo, the star, which they saw in the east, went before them, till it came and stood over where the young child was.*
*10 When they saw the star, they rejoiced with exceeding great joy.*
*11 And when they were come into the house, they saw the young child with Mary his mother, and fell down, and worshipped him: and when they had opened their treasures, they presented unto him gifts; gold, and frankincense and myrrh.*
*12 And being warned of God in a dream that they should not return to Herod, they departed into their own country another way.*
*13 And when they were departed, behold, the angel of the Lord appeareth to Joseph in a dream, saying, Arise, and take the young child and his mother, and flee into Egypt, and be thou there until I bring thee word: for Herod will seek the young child to destroy him.*
*14 When he arose, he took the young child and his mother by night, and departed into Egypt:*
*15 And was there until the death of Herod: that it might be fulfilled which was spoken of the Lord by the prophet, saying, Out of Egypt have I called my son.*
*16 Then Herod, when he saw that he was mocked of the wise men, was exceeding wroth, and sent forth, and slew all the children that were in Bethlehem, and in all the coasts thereof, from two years old and under, according to the time which he had diligently inquired of the wise men.*
*17 Then was fulfilled that which was spoken by Jeremiah the prophet, saying,*
*18 In Rama was there a voice heard, lamentation, and weeping, and great mourning, Rachel weeping for her children, and would not be comforted, because they are not.*
*19 But when Herod was dead, behold, an angel of the Lord appeareth in a dream to Joseph in Egypt,*
*20 Saying, Arise, and take the young child and his mother, and go into the land of Israel: for they are dead which sought the young child's life.*
*21 And he arose, and took the young child and his mother, and came into the land of Israel.*
*22 But when he heard that Archelaus did reign in Judaea in the room of his father Herod, he was afraid to go thither: notwithstanding, being warned of God in a dream, he turned aside into the parts of Galilee:*
*23 And he came and dwelt in a city called Nazareth: that it might be fulfilled which was spoken by the prophets, He shall be called a Nazarene.*

Sorry to be so late, what a day I had. And thankfully, Matthew 2 is a very straightforward chapter. The call backs to prophetic scripture in the birth of Jesus continue, establishing the testimony that Jesus is the Christ foretold.

We see the wise men of the east, who came seeking Jesus at his birth, who are not Hebrews, and yet aware of the promise of God and who worshiped him, bestowing gifts of kings. As we saw in chapter 1, by right, Jesus was King of the Jews.

Herod, in jealous anger repeated the horror of pharoah, and the murder of the male children under his rule, as was done in the days of Moses.

At the angels behest, Joseph takes Jesus and Mary to Egypt, eventually returning again in fulfillment of scripture. In many ways echoing the story of Moses, yet to deliver us spiritually to the promised land rather than the physical salvation of Exodus.

**John 5:28-29**

 *Marvel not at this: for the hour is coming, in the which all that are in the graves shall hear his voice, And shall come forth; they that have done good, unto the resurrection of life; and they that have done evil, unto the resurrection of damnation*.

**Matthew 3**

*In those days came John the Baptist, preaching in the wilderness of Judaea,*

*2 And saying, Repent ye: for the kingdom of heaven is at hand.*

*3 For this is he that was spoken of by the prophet Esaias, saying, The voice of one crying in the wilderness, Prepare ye the way of the Lord, make his paths straight.*

*4 And the same John had his raiment of camel's hair, and a leathern girdle about his loins; and his meat was locusts and wild honey.*

*5 Then went out to him Jerusalem, and all Judaea, and all the region round about Jordan,*

*6 And were baptized of him in Jordan, confessing their sins.*

*7 But when he saw many of the Pharisees and Sadducees come to his baptism, he said unto them, O generation of vipers, who hath warned you to flee from the wrath to come?*

*8 Bring forth therefore fruits meet for repentance:*

*9 And think not to say within yourselves, We have Abraham to our father: for I say unto you, that God is able of these stones to raise up children unto Abraham.*

*10 And now also the axe is laid unto the root of the trees: therefore every tree which bringeth not forth good fruit is hewn down, and cast into the fire.*

*11 I indeed baptize you with water unto repentance. but he that cometh after me is mightier than I, whose shoes I am not worthy to bear: he shall baptize you with the Holy Ghost, and with fire:*

*12 Whose fan is in his hand, and he will throughly purge his floor, and gather his wheat into the garner; but he will burn up the chaff with unquenchable fire.*

*13 Then cometh Jesus from Galilee to Jordan unto John, to be baptized of him.*

*14 But John forbad him, saying, I have need to be baptized of thee, and comest thou to me?*

*15 And Jesus answering said unto him, Suffer it to be so now: for thus it becometh us to fulfil all righteousness. Then he suffered him.*

*16 And Jesus, when he was baptized, went up straightway out of the water: and, lo, the heavens were opened unto him, and he saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove, and lighting upon him:*

*17 And lo a voice from heaven, saying, This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.*

The prophet who comes before Christ. The voice crying out in the wilderness. Telling all men to turn towards God, that the Messiah is coming. John the Baptist.

Jesus cousin, raised by his righteous parents, bringing people to salvation and baptising believers, by immersion, in much water.

Baptism not being the putting away of sin, but the answer of a good conscience by those who have called upon the name of the Lord for forgiveness of sin and everlasting life. The same unbroken line of faith from John to modern, NT Christians. (Note it's not John the Catholic or John the Lutheran)

He eschews comfort. Eats ze bugs. And rips face with hard preaching. Matthew 3 captures a moment of John's style of fire-breathing, hellfire and damnation preaching, in this case against the Pharisees and Sadducees. The religious leaders of Judea, come down to be seen where the actions at. Maybe to be baptized to seem holy. But John calls them out.

*O generation of vipers, who hath warned you to flee from the wrath to come? Bring forth therefore fruits meet for repentance: And think not to say within yourselves, We have Abraham to our father: for I say unto you, that God is able of these stones to raise up children unto Abraham.And now also the axe is laid unto the root of the trees: therefore every tree which bringeth not forth good fruit is hewn down, and cast into the fire.*

Much as Jesus would later, as detailed in Matthew 7 and 23, he calls out these hypocrites, this generation of vipers, false preachers who bear bad fruit. Not souls won, ready to accept Christ. They bring forth no fruit, thistles. False prophets, which come to you in sheep's clothing, but inwardly they are ravening wolves.

Then he goes after their reliance on being special boys, born from Abraham, saying God could make a rock a son of Abraham. That their being Jews isn't going to save them. (RIP Dispensationalism).

He tells these reprobate hypocrites that Jesus who's coming, will sort them like chafe from wheat, into the fire. Cut down their tree, throw it in the fire. Brimstone-throwing preaching. Amen!

And Jesus, our Lord comes, whose shoes we aren't worthy to unlatch. And he goes down into the water, and straightway rises up out of the water with the Holy Ghost upon Him. And the blessing of the Father is given to the Son. Amen.
I can't begin to understand any saved Christian who doesn't like hellfire and brimstone hard preaching, against sin. Against wickedness.

**Matthew 4**

*Then was Jesus led up of the Spirit into the wilderness to be tempted of the devil.*

*2 And when he had fasted forty days and forty nights, he was afterward an hungred.*

*3 And when the tempter came to him, he said, If thou be the Son of God, command that these stones be made bread.*

*4 But he answered and said, It is written, Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of God.*

*5 Then the devil taketh him up into the holy city, and setteth him on a pinnacle of the temple,*

*6 And saith unto him, If thou be the Son of God, cast thyself down: for it is written, He shall give his angels charge concerning thee: and in their hands they shall bear thee up, lest at any time thou dash thy foot against a stone.*

*7 Jesus said unto him, It is written again, Thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God.*

*8 Again, the devil taketh him up into an exceeding high mountain, and sheweth him all the kingdoms of the world, and the glory of them;*

*9 And saith unto him, All these things will I give thee, if thou wilt fall down and worship me.*

*10 Then saith Jesus unto him, Get thee hence, Satan: for it is written, Thou shalt worship the Lord thy God, and him only shalt thou serve.*

*11 Then the devil leaveth him, and, behold, angels came and ministered unto him.*

*12 Now when Jesus had heard that John was cast into prison, he departed into Galilee;*

*13 And leaving Nazareth, he came and dwelt in Capernaum, which is upon the sea coast, in the borders of Zabulon and Nephthalim:*

*14 That it might be fulfilled which was spoken by Esaias the prophet, saying,*

*15 The land of Zabulon, and the land of Nephthalim, by the way of the sea, beyond Jordan, Galilee of the Gentiles;*

*16 The people which sat in darkness saw great light; and to them which sat in the region and shadow of death light is sprung up.*

*17 From that time Jesus began to preach, and to say, Repent: for the kingdom of heaven is at hand.*

*18 And Jesus, walking by the sea of Galilee, saw two brethren, Simon called Peter, and Andrew his brother, casting a net into the sea: for they were fishers.*

*19 And he saith unto them, Follow me, and I will make you fishers of men.*

*20 And they straightway left their nets, and followed him.*

*21 And going on from thence, he saw other two brethren, James the son of Zebedee, and John his brother, in a ship with Zebedee their father, mending their nets; and he called them.*

*22 And they immediately left the ship and their father, and followed him.*

*23 And Jesus went about all Galilee, teaching in their synagogues, and preaching the gospel of the kingdom, and healing all manner of sickness and all manner of disease among the people.*

*24 And his fame went throughout all Syria: and they brought unto him all sick people that were taken with divers diseases and torments, and those which were possessed with devils, and those which were lunatick, and those that had the palsy; and he healed them.*

*25 And there followed him great multitudes of people from Galilee, and from Decapolis, and from Jerusalem, and from Judaea, and from beyond Jordan.*

Following Jesus' baptism and the announcement of the Father that this was His Son in Whom He was well pleased and the anointing by the Holy Ghost, Jesus went into the wilderness to fast. Knowing hunger, being in the flesh, He was tested and tried of all things and yet sinless.

When Satan came and likewise tempted Him with rewards of the flesh, twisting scripture to do it, Jesus cites the word to both rebuke the devil and keep Himself pure.

This is how Satan attacks us all. He wanders the earth like a ravening lion, seeking who he can devour. He is before God the Father accusing believers, day and night. He gets us to give in to lusts of the flesh, and if possible, gets us to justify it as God's will by twisting His word. Same as with Eve in the garden. Same as with the Son of God in the wilderness.

And unlike Eve, Jesus rebuke sends the devil packing, defeated and angels are sent to minister to Christ.

Matthew then tells the story of the beginning of Jesus' ministry, the recruitment of some of the apostles from Galilee, having gone there to avoid Judea after the arrest of John the Baptist.

The willingness of the apostles to leave father, home, job, everything to follow Christ is an example to all believers and seekers. As we know from Gospel of John, they were seeking the Messiah of the prophets already, and heard their master's voice when He called. Knowing the scriptures, they knew His word, and the promise and so, when called heard His voice.

This is why we are reminded that scripture said that man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of God. It's Jesus' first lesson to us. We live by His word.

**Matthew 5**

*And seeing the multitudes, he went up into a mountain: and when he was set, his disciples came unto him:*

*2 And he opened his mouth, and taught them, saying,*

*3 Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.*

*4 Blessed are they that mourn: for they shall be comforted.*

*5 Blessed are the meek: for they shall inherit the earth.*

*6 Blessed are they which do hunger and thirst after righteousness: for they shall be filled.*

*7 Blessed are the merciful: for they shall obtain mercy.*

*8 Blessed are the pure in heart: for they shall see God.*

*23 Therefore if thou bring thy gift to the altar, and there rememberest that thy brother hath ought against thee;*

*24 Leave there thy gift before the altar, and go thy way; first be reconciled to thy brother, and then come and offer thy gift.*

*25 Agree with thine adversary quickly, whiles thou art in the way with him; lest at any time the adversary deliver thee to the judge, and the judge deliver thee to the officer, and thou be cast into prison.*

*26 Verily I say unto thee, Thou shalt by no means come out thence, till thou hast paid the uttermost farthing.*

*27 Ye have heard that it was said by them of old time, Thou shalt not commit adultery:*

*28 But I say unto you, That whosoever looketh on a woman to lust after her hath committed adultery with her already in his heart.*

*29 And if thy right eye offend thee, pluck it out, and cast it from thee: for it is profitable for thee that one of thy members should perish, and not that thy whole body should be cast into hell.*

*30 And if thy right hand offend thee, cut it off, and cast it from thee: for it is profitable for thee that one of thy members should perish, and not that thy whole body should be cast into hell.*

*31 It hath been said, Whosoever shall put away his wife, let him give her a writing of divorcement:*

*32 But I say unto you, That whosoever shall put away his wife, saving for the cause of fornication, causeth her to commit adultery: and whosoever shall marry her that is divorced committeth adultery.*

*33 Again, ye have heard that it hath been said by them of old time, Thou shalt not forswear thyself, but shalt perform unto the Lord thine oaths:*

*34 But I say unto you, Swear not at all; neither by heaven; for it is God's throne:*

*35 Nor by the earth; for it is his footstool: neither by Jerusalem; for it is the city of the great King.*

*36 Neither shalt thou swear by thy head, because thou canst not make one hair white or black.*

*37 But let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay: for whatsoever is more than these cometh of evil.*

*38 Ye have heard that it hath been said, An eye for an eye, and a tooth for a tooth:*

*40 And if any man will sue thee at the law, and take away thy coat, let him have thy cloak also.*

*41 And whosoever shall compel thee to go a mile, go with him twain.*

*42 Give to him that asketh thee, and from him that would borrow of thee turn not thou away.*

*43 Ye have heard that it hath been said, Thou shalt love thy neighbour, and hate thine enemy.*

*44 But I say unto you, Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you, and pray for them which despitefully use you, and persecute you;*

*45 That ye may be the children of your Father which is in heaven: for he maketh his sun to rise on the evil and on the good, and sendeth rain on the just and on the unjust.*

*47 And if ye salute your brethren only, what do ye more than others? do not even the publicans so?*

**Matthew 5**

*And seeing the multitudes, he went up into a mountain: and when he was set, his disciples came unto him:*

*2 And he opened his mouth, and taught them, saying,*

*3 Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.*

*4 Blessed are they that mourn: for they shall be comforted.*

*5 Blessed are the meek: for they shall inherit the earth.*

*6 Blessed are they which do hunger and thirst after righteousness: for they shall be filled.*

*7 Blessed are the merciful: for they shall obtain mercy.*

*8 Blessed are the pure in heart: for they shall see God.*

*9 Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God.*

*10 Blessed are they which are persecuted for righteousness' sake: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.*

*11 Blessed are ye, when men shall revile you, and persecute you, and shall say all manner of evil against you falsely, for my sake.*

*12 Rejoice, and be exceeding glad: for great is your reward in heaven: for so persecuted they the prophets which were before you.*

Here in Matthew 5 we are given a taste of the preaching of Jesus. The themes and doctrines which Jesus taught in this sermon on the mount, starting with what are called the beatitudes, the blessings of those with certain traits pleasing to God.

The poor in spirit, even the least of the saved, are partakers of the inheritance, the Kingdom of Heaven.

Those that mourn, longing for those loved ones sleeping in Christ will have a comforter in the Holy Spirit, and in the promise of the resurrection.

The meek, those who humble themselves before the Lord and live with that understanding of their status as inheritors being only by grace and mercy from God, not of their own deeds.

Those who hunger and thirst for righteousness will be filled. Those who earnestly seek salvation, His wisdom, the imputed righteousness of Jesus, God promises it will be given to them. And that we will drink of the living water of Christ and never thirst again, eat of the bread that is Jesus, and never hunger.

The merciful will receive mercy, the pure of heart will see God. It is that mercy from God that makes us pure of heart.

Blessed are the peacemakers, they are the children of God. Not the children of the darkness, of disobedience but the children of the light, who obey the Gospel and share it with others, bringing peace to them with God in His goodwill. Making peace with our enemies, and heaping coals upon their heads. Making peace with the beloved, so we may have unity in the members of the body of Christ, following the head that is Jesus.

And blessed are we who may be persecuted for His name's sake. For the cause of Christ.

Saved Christians are these things, and these blessings are a promise to those faithful that we should strive to exemplify that we may fully receive the inheritance and blessings as a child of God.

Throughout scripture we see that the children of man are given a share of inheritance and a blessing for their future, and God is no different a Father. We are blessed with reward beyond measure, eternal life, filled with His righteousness. Let's redeem the time and not squander the gifts by being contrary to these ideals.

**Matthew 5** continues

*13 Ye are the salt of the earth: but if the salt have lost his savour, wherewith shall it be salted? it is thenceforth good for nothing, but to be cast out, and to be trodden under foot of men.*

*14 Ye are the light of the world. A city that is set on an hill cannot be hid.*

*15 Neither do men light a candle, and put it under a bushel, but on a candlestick; and it giveth light unto all that are in the house.*

*16 Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father which is in heaven.*

Jesus addresses the Jews to whom He's preaching, and reminds them of the Israelites' role in being chosen by God, to be the example. A light unto the world. To be the salt of the earth giving savor to God's word, bringing it to all men. And having lost that purpose, being worthless and cast out.

All those who call themselves by His name are called to this ministry, and all risk the same end of being trampled under foot if they lose their savor. Hide their light. Not winning souls and providing living examples of the power of the gospel. No longer giving off the glory of God to guide the lost.

*17 Think not that I am come to destroy the law, or the prophets: I am not come to destroy, but to fulfil.*

*18 For verily I say unto you, Till heaven and earth pass, one jot or one tittle shall in no wise pass from the law, till all be fulfilled.*

*19 Whosoever therefore shall break one of these least commandments, and shall teach men so, he shall be called the least in the kingdom of heaven: but whosoever shall do and teach them, the same shall be called great in the kingdom of heaven.*

*20 For I say unto you, That except your righteousness shall exceed the righteousness of the scribes and Pharisees, ye shall in no case enter into the kingdom of heaven.*

Jesus tells us that the law of God, being perfect and preserved, isn't being upended by what He preached or His eventual death and resurrection, but fulfilling all things in the end. That all shall be made subject to Him, the earth as His footstool and the promise of the Kingdom kept for the children of God. The Jews hearing this being familiar with scripture, knowing the law, the prophets and the promise, would understand, at least those with ears to hear. Those seeking righteousness.

Unlike the claimed righteousness of the scribes and Pharisees, who taught loopholes and exceptions to God's law and accused Jesus of seeking to destroy it, we must have the righteousness of Christ to enter into the Kingdom of Heaven, exceeding those hypocrites' false idea of righteousness.

**Matthew 6**

*7 But when ye pray, use not vain repetitions, as the heathen do: for they think that they shall be heard for their much speaking.*

*8 Be not ye therefore like unto them: for your Father knoweth what things ye have need of, before ye ask him.*

*9 After this manner therefore pray ye: Our Father which art in heaven, Hallowed be thy name.*

*10 Thy kingdom come, Thy will be done in earth, as it is in heaven.*

*11 Give us this day our daily bread.*

*12 And forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors.*

The false idea that Jesus came to liberalize the law rather than liberate us from the law is part and parcel to the works crowd's self-righteous theology.

That divorce is adultery. That other than putting away a betrothed before the consummation due to her or her parents lying about her chastity, that she had fornicated, there was no sufficient reason to not marry the woman to whom you'd pledged yourself, and cleaved unto.

In cases of premarital fornication, the male partner was meant to pay a dowry and make her his wife, having taken her honor. Note that fornication, a grievous sin, has remedy under God's perfect law that satisfies all parties involved, while discouraging the practice. Whereas adultery is met with a death sentence, it's being a crime.

And so we are here in Matthew 20, and Jesus tells His disciples a parable. Of a man, hiring hands for the harvest, where each is given the agreed upon wage, a penny for a day's work. Those that labored from the start, and even those who labored but a short time. And the longest among them grumbled that they should receive the same reward.

But entrance to the Kingdom of Heaven is the reward itself, agreed upon in faith, and contentions of who will be greatest therein is up to the judgment of God the Father, and our own judgment of our own works does not give us the right to question this.

Believing Jews in the newly forming churches saw themselves as "first," the Gentiles, "last." Often prideful and puffed-up Christians, having been born to believers and raised in a church will look down on babes in Christ, coming from a sinful past and yet to get right in all things.

Those who volunteer at church, and attend 3 times a week. Who carry all the chairs and make the largest pot luck. Who show for soul winning times, and go on mission trips, spreading the Gospel, but not out of humility of being a servant. Not out of satisfaction of being least, and thus, doing all things from that meek humility of the recognition of their retched state, but instead out of striving and contention. Pride.

Good works done, and some reward had, for certain, when the fire burns away the wood, hay and stubble, some diamonds will surely remain. But yet, how much the greater their reward if they had become like unto children? Had been ministers to others. Willing and happy servants?

This is the lesson Jesus tries to teach His disciples, and was preparing them to see Him live out, in Jerusalem.

Now the sons of Zebedee, James and John (whom Jesus nicknames 'Boanerges,' which means "Sons of Thunder” (**Mark 3:17**) were part of His core inner circle, along with Peter. They witnessed the transfiguration on the mount. James was the first to follow Christ's example of being willing to die for Him, and was first of them to be martyred. John, living the longest, writing His gospel, the revelation of Jesus, and passing from old age, the only one of the original 12 to do so. Truly they were great men of God.

Here, in this context of the last and the first, the martyrs and servants, those who lose everything to gain Christ, and His impending sacrifice, that their mother comes asking, "*Grant that these my two sons may sit, the one on thy right hand, and the other on the left, in thy kingdom.*" And Jesus replies that she doesn't understand what she is asking for them. That to obtain such position isn't His to give, but the price is higher than perhaps a mother could ever grieve for their sons.

"*Are ye able to drink of the cup that I shall drink of, and to be baptized with the baptism that I am baptized with?*" Jesus asks them, signifying the manner of death that awaited Him. And, the Bible says, they replied, "*We are able*."

Perhaps it is out of mercy that God only held one brother to that fate, and used the other for some of His greatest work on earth, writing the definitive Gospel of faith that unbelievers should know salvation, and revealing to John the manner of the end of the world, in his old age.

James however wasn't spared. One wonders if his mother was alive to see it, and if she made peace, knowing finally what it was she had asked.

Now this exchange causes the other 10 to strive with the 2 brothers. Jesus pleas with them to not engage in that kind of dispute over who is greater.

He says that the princes of this world exercise authority by who is greater, who has the most, commands the most. But that in His kingdom it isn't so.

"*Whosoever will be chief among you, let him be your servant: Even as the Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister, and to give his life a ransom for many*."

This still applies today. Jesus did not come here to bring peace, but division. Separation. Among family. Among friends. From wealth and personal comfort. That we will see tribulations and persecution. And to be hated by man for His name.

The promise is that *every one that hath forsaken houses, or brethren, or sisters, or father, or mother, or wife, or children, or lands, for my name's sake, shall receive an hundredfold.* That tribulation in this world is glory in the next. That being meek, poor in spirit, but great in faith, willing to suffer that others may gain, is how we are to live, and great is the reward for those of us who may.

To be servants. To wash the feet of others. To be ministers. Not puffed up. But as like unto a child. To show mercy for others, not being proud of our own righteousness but a reflection of Christ's.

And as they pass two blind beggars, persistent in their faith, Jesus has mercy upon them, and they are given their sight.

The blind made to see.

If you, like I, struggle occasionally on this lesson, how to be humble. How not to resent our status, position, wealth and comfort. How to live for Christ as a minister to the weak, with no expectations for added reward, but happy with the gift of eternal life we have hope on, listening to the Spirit with the new man inside, pray. Pray and worship, persistently. Asking Jesus to be able to see.

First, let us rightly divide the word of God here, it isn't regarding salvation of a person's soul, rather this is directed at the nation of Israel which had put their faith in idols, facing the abominations set before them in service to false gods.

*20 And the rest of the men which were not killed by these plagues yet repented not of the works of their hands, that they should not worship devils, and idols of gold, and silver, and brass, and stone, and of wood: which neither can see, nor hear, nor walk:*

Repentance as preached by John the Baptist, Jesus Christ and the Apostles was not an act or work. It was not about behavior or feelings. Neither a prerequisite *to* nor a consequence *of* salvation. but was actually *the very expression of faith* in Jesus Christ and bringing salvation to those who have thus repented.

John 3:16 says *For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son, that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have everlasting life.*

Is there a biblical example of repentance from sin? Of turning from, with fresh information changing ones mind, turning towards the correct action in regards to stopping sinful behavior? Yes.

But it's not regarding getting saved (not directly), but of those who had already believed getting right.

In 1 Corinthians, Paul wrote to the saints in Corinth regarding the open fornication among them, and their taking one another to court for petty disputes, among other things. He ripped into them, that they ought to know better and to repent of it, to think better of it. To come to the realization that it is wrong and hurt their ability to do God's will in sharing the gospel, while they had such sin among them.

And in 2 Corinthians, written a year or so later, Paul tells us by way of praising them, that they had repented of it.

*5 For, when we were come into Macedonia, our flesh had no rest, but we were troubled on every side; without were fightings, within were fears.*

*10 For godly sorrow worketh repentance to salvation not to be repented of: but the sorrow of the world worketh death.*

*11 For behold this selfsame thing, that ye sorrowed after a godly sort, what carefulness it wrought in you, yea, what clearing of yourselves, yea, what indignation, yea, what fear, yea, what vehement desire, yea, what zeal, yea, what revenge! In all things ye have approved yourselves to be clear in this matter.*

*12 Wherefore, though I wrote unto you, I did it not for his cause that had done the wrong, nor for his cause that suffered wrong, but that our care for you in the sight of God might appear unto you.*

*13 Therefore we were comforted in your comfort: yea, and exceedingly the more joyed we for the joy of Titus, because his spirit was refreshed by you all.*

Note in verse 10, Paul is giving us a general rule, that godly sorrow, that is sincerely being sorry at a wrong you've done, leads many to the repentance of belief that is salvation, while the sorrow of this world to death.

In other words, being sorry you were caught, sorry you're in trouble, sorry you're paying a price for it, sorry that God has chastised you, this is worldly sorrow, and in it is death, because it isn't genuine, it's selfish.

Paul says, godly sorrow, truly understanding the harm done to others or to God by our transgressions, can lead to repentance towards salvation, a change of mind that cannot be repented of. Faith in Christ, that cannot be lost once gained. Once saved, always saved.

But to the Corinthians, who had already tasted the good word of God, tasted the heavenly gift, and the powers of the world to come, partakers of the Holy Ghost, as they'd already come to repentance unto salvation. The Bible says, *it is impossible...to renew them again unto repentance; seeing they crucify to themselves the Son of God afresh, and put him to an open shame.*

So Paul isn't telling the Corinthians that their turning from the sin he pointed out among them is how they were saved, for they were already, but makes this comment as a part of a larger point, regarding their acceptance of his rebuke.

But to focus on this a moment, as it is the only clear verse on the matter of "repenting of sin" in regards to salvation, note that this sincere sorrow for sin is not itself repentance, but rather, repentance is the work of that sorrow. That some may come to understanding of the faith by which we must believe to be justified by the sorrow for those they have wronged and the life that they've led. The regret. The penitent believer.

Because, the Bible says of some, we *save with fear, pulling them out of the fire; hating even the garment spotted by the flesh*. Amen, this is the case of many, brought to repent unto Christ for the forgiveness of sins, and relief from the godly sorrow and guilt weighing their conscience, lifted up by the Holy Spirit and the surety of the promise.

But again, that's not the only thing that wortheth repentance. *For some have compassion, making a difference,* our caring and meekness, our ready answer for our hope, our chaste conversation, our example, the light of Jesus Christ shining through us, bring many to repentance as well.

As many receive it in tears, many still receive the truth in joy.

The circumstance and situation, the seed planted, the watering, the harvesting, the condition of the soil and the time of the season varies. But the repentance, the acceptance of the truth and the salvation earned remains the same, in sorrow and tears, or in laughter and joy.

There is more valuable doctrine on repentance of sin to be had in this chapter, the change of mind with new information from Paul's first epistle and realization by the Corinthians, that what were doing that was wrong. Their godly sorrow leading to their getting right with God. The accompanying signs of genuinely changing their minds. In chapter 11, Paul lists the ways by which he knows they truly were sorry.

Paul writes; *For behold this selfsame thing, that ye sorrowed after a godly sort, what carefulness it wrought in you, yea, what clearing of yourselves, yea, what indignation, yea, what fear, yea, what vehement desire, yea, what zeal, yea, what revenge! In all things ye have approved yourselves to be clear in this matter.*

He says this selfsame thing, this godly sorrow that may led one to salvation, is evident in them. He determines that they took his rebuke in the spirit it was intended and it manifested in their change of heart, which he sees (through the report of Titus), in that the rebuke and the sincere sorrow it caused led them to be *careful*; to take care and paying attention to the matter and the implications there of.
To a *clearing of themselves*, that is getting right, to strive for being blameless, in this and in other possible sin. The *indignation* they felt towards themselves, the outrage at their own failings. The *fear,* of the chastisement from God, and the natural repercussions of their actions. The *zeal, the vehement desire,* by which they sought to get right, *the revenge* they took upon themselves, making good on the restitution of their error.

These signs by which Paul acquits them, that *ye have approved yourselves to be clear in this matter.*

This is a helpful list, both for those us us seeking to get right with God regarding sin in our life, and how we should act, and for judging rightly the sincerity, be it godly or earthly sorrow, of those who have wronged us and are seeking forgiveness and claim to be making amends.

Genuine godly sorrow and a turning from a sin, or sins should produce a carefulness surrounding the behavior, an understanding of what it is you've done, how it affects others, the ripple effects and implications for the harm you've caused, and the things that lead you to the sin, whatever it may be. Not giving occasion to the flesh.

It should lead to a clearing of yourself. An assessment of not just this particular sin, but of how you may be perceived by those around you, to whom you need make restitution, and others caught up in the wake of our iniquities. To make yourself as blameless as possible going forward, in careful consideration.

You should be indignant at what you've done. Outraged at yourself. Embarrassed by the shame, hating even the garment spotted by the flesh. Despising that about you that led to your sin.

And having a vehement desire and zeal for reformation, taking revenge against yourself, which here means making an honest retribution for the harm caused, not begrudgingly, but with zeal. Willingly and needfully making things right, as your vehement desire.

Now note again, these all are the fruits of godly sorrow, just as repentance is the coming to understanding, in this case through that sorrow. They are not the same thing.

It is the conflating of regret/godly sorrow/understanding of our sinful nature and the wages of death earned by it, with the actual change of mind, turning to faith in God, in Christ for our salvation, upon which bad doctrine and damnable heresies are founded.

"What must I do to be saved?"

*Believe on the Lord Jesus Christ and thou shall be saved*.

*That if thou shalt confess with thy mouth the Lord Jesus, and shalt believe in thine heart that God hath raised him from the dead, thou shalt be saved*.

This is what we must repent towards, to believe to be saved.

Regardless of how we get to the point of repentance, of taking the truth we hear and believing it, in our heart, turning towards God.

Not of sin, though godly sorrow for sin may lead us there. Not of any works, or deeds of the law. Not of our sincere, careful, vehement desire to make right what we've done wrong in godly sorrow. These may work us to the change of heart and towards faith, but they aren't requirements for salvation, which is to believe on Jesus Christ, that He was raised from the dead.

Some call upon the name of the Lord while in tribulation, being beset by the wicked and surrounded by enemies. In desperation, stricken by poor health, or in mourning for a loved one. By example of the righteous being kind and compassionate to them in their hour of need. Of being fed and clothed by believers, when they had nothing and hungered. Of seeing God's light magnified in the kindness and charity, mercy and faith of we who believe.

The Bible tells us of many circumstance that brings a sinner to repentance towards God. It is not always of guilt and shame. Making it so excludes many from receiving the Gospel, and the prominence of this doctrine, making repentance of sin the way to be born again, places the onus of salvation, of being justified, upon the would-be believers to clean up their act. It implies that this is the means of salvation, their ability to do the works of the law. It becomes works salvation, either before the fact, or after, to show "genuine repentance," to maintain salvation, or as proof it was real.

To both backslidden believers and the unregenerate sinner who had already 'cleaned up their life,' and had genuine sorrow and repented of their sins, but not believed on Christ, it places a stumbling block.

It is a wicked heresy for this very reason. And that is why Satan pushes it so hard.

I think one of the stumbling blocks for those who have come to repentance via their genuine sorrow for sins, those that hit bottom, so to speak, seeing their lives and relationships destroyed by their own selfish and destructive behavior, and having a rocky path to making things right, is that there are resentments for those who come to the faith by other means.

There are many who are raised Christian, in godly homes, and can't even tell you when they believed.

There are many who, when they heard the truth, accepted it. Absent trauma or drama, and yet saved.

There are those who had long ago cleaned up their act, dealt with their addictions, or put away the anger and hurt at being victimized, say by abuse, physical, sexual or emotional. That turned over a new leaf, and yet only believed on the Gospel years after.

And there are those, caught in the jaws of addiction, struggling to get out, long after repenting of what led them there, but unable to break free, who are comforted by a believer, and asking them, are given the Gospel and while yet, still sinners, in a moment of clarity, believe.

People who crawled through whatever hell on earth to come to salvation, by sorrow for their sin, can look at these disparate cases, and others like them, and think "that person is not really saved, like I am."

And the promotion of the idea that we must repent of our sins to be saved feeds that resentment, and can make a repentant heart grow bitter over time.

This resentment is similar to the workers who labored all day for the same penny that those late arrivals collected in the parable Jesus tells in Matthew 20. It's sort of the inverse reaction of the good son in the parable of the prodigal son.

It's this attitude that leads to holier than thou fruit inspectors, judging others salvation by their works, being a respecter of persons regarding testimonials, etc.

Before heading in to Matthew chapter 23, it's a good idea to consider how hypocrisy flourishes from the idea of salvation by repentance from sin, rather than repentance towards God and faith in Christ.

By placing the emphasis on what was turned from, rather than the testimony of what is turned to, what the changing of mind has wrought through faith, it creates an almost inevitable form of a caste system within a church. Of respecters of persons, who in hypocrisy see themselves as *more saved* than others.

Just as the apostles asking Jesus of whose sin was responsible for the man blind from birth, or those questioning him about the men killed by Pilate, are those who had a wall fall on them killing them, the tendency and inclination to place the path to righteousness some take over the experience of others is the same form of hypocrisy which Jesus warns us against.

For all have sinned and fallen short of the glory of God. For all were perishing before repenting to believe on Christ. For all are deserving of hell, and none are justified by their works of the law.

We are all in the same boat and there but for the grace of God go each and every one of us. Regardless of how relatively easy we came to salvation, and regardless of how we struggle to pick up our cross daily and follow him.

And losing sight of that leads to our focusing on the mote of our neighbor's eye. Of neglecting the beam in our own. Of judging in hypocrisy the Christian walk of others, while neglecting to work out our own salvation in fear and trembling.

This is one reason why I dislike so-called testimonial preaching. Not the testimony of Jesus Christ and the saving power of faith, but the long winded testimonials, almost reveling in past sin, showing you just how down low someone was before receiving the gospel, almost a point of pride of how much they had to dig themselves out to get to where others are mercifully, by the grace of God.

And I have been in churches where this becomes almost a competition of sorts. And where people blessed to have been born into a Godly family, and whose sowing of wild oats was almost incidental, making it out to be that they were low down wretched creatures, by way of showing just how really super duper saved they are, through their "struggle." Who haven't been blessed by God's grace and mercy, are embarrassed by it, for the glory that is heaped upon those with a testimony of a life of sin, turned around.

This is yet another reason why Satan has painstakingly and methodically brainwashed everyone into adding "...of sin" to repentance. It's another way this becomes toxic in even good churches, with the right Gospel.

We should not glory in the fact that those more sinful than we were saved. We should glory in God that he would save any of us. We were all equally damned. We all had to turn to believe the same thing to gain life. One sin or millions. A degenerate life in the swinehurd, for a life of ease and comfort of our father's estate.

For all have fallen short of the glory of God and deserve death and Hell.

But God has sent his servants to invite us to his Son's wedding feast, both good and bad, called to repentance. Amen
